clue.text: Painters mad about job involving dancing

indicators.note: about places the rearranged letters around the next piece, as a container
mad suggests the letters of Painters have gone wild and must be rearranged

parts.note: a chore is a household job or task

explanation.surface: Some deranged house painters are tackling a job that somehow involves dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mad' turns PAINTERS into TERPSIAN, and 'about' wraps that round CHORE, splitting it after TERPSI. Terpsichore is the Muse of dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Terpsichore was the Greek Muse of dance, so the adjective from her name describes anything to do with dancing.

clue.text: Sly entertainment

parts.note: Christopher Sly is the drunken tinker in the induction of a Shakespeare comedy, for whom the main play is staged as an entertainment

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sly' looks like an adjective (cunning); it is the name of the character for whom Shakespeare's play-within-a-play is performed.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's comedy is put on as a play for the tinker Christopher Sly, tricked into believing he is a lord.

clue.text: Birds round Tattenham Corner for instance

definitions.meaning: wading marsh birds of the crake family such as the water rail
the fences lining a racecourse, as on Tattenham Corner, the famous bend on Epsom Downs where the Derby is run

explanation.walkthrough: Tattenham Corner is the sharp left-hand bend at Epsom racecourse, home of the Derby; horses hug the barriers there.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share one word: a family of marsh birds, and the barriers lining a horse-racing track.

clue.text: How maliciously King Gama poked sarcastic jokes

definitions.text: How maliciously King Gama poked sarcastic jokes

parts.words: How maliciously King Gama poked sarcastic jokes
parts.note: King Gama in Gilbert and Sullivan's Princess Ida is a sour, disagreeable monarch whose barbs are full of malice

explanation.walkthrough: King Gama, of Gilbert and Sullivan's Princess Ida, sings of being thought 'such a disagreeable man'; the clue simply asks for the adverb describing his mocking manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something with malice and ill will is doing it in a vindictive, nasty way.

clue.text: In song my darling one, Rachel, in distress

indicators.note: in distress tells us these letters are troubled and disordered, so rearranged

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A singer's darling Rachel is weeping and upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in distress' scrambles I (one) and RACHEL. 'Charlie Is My Darling' is a Jacobite song about Bonnie Prince Charlie.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish Jacobite song is titled Charlie Is My Darling, naming the prince as the singer's beloved.

clue.text: Hard to bear, one endless drinking-bout

indicators.note: endless means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a rouse is an old word for a carousal or bout of heavy drinking

explanation.surface: One long night of drinking that never stops is hard to put up with.
explanation.walkthrough: ROUSE (an archaic word for a bumper or carousal, used in Hamlet) loses its last letter by 'endless', giving ROUS.
explanation.definitionFit: A burdensome or heavy duty is one that is difficult to carry.

clue.text: "It is the ——, and Juliet is the sun" (R & J)

definitions.text: It is the ——, and Juliet is the sun" (R & J)

parts.words: It is the ——, and Juliet is the sun" (R & J)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Romeo's balcony speech, where the window Juliet appears at is the quarter of sunrise

explanation.walkthrough: Romeo, seeing light at Juliet's window, says 'But soft! what light through yonder window breaks? It is the ___, and Juliet is the sun.' R & J is Romeo and Juliet.
explanation.definitionFit: The sun rises in that quarter, so Romeo names the compass point of dawn for the window.

clue.text: Story about the right renegade is ingenuous

indicators.note: about sets one word around the following pieces, as a container

parts.note: naive means innocent, ingenuous
a rat is a deserter or renegade

explanation.surface: A tale about a right-wing turncoat is dismissed as naive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts NAIVE around R and RAT, splitting it after NA.
explanation.definitionFit: An account of events, told as a tale, is a story.

clue.text: Bird in Cornish fraternity has a sharp appetite

parts.note: Cornwall lies in the South-West of England, abbreviated SW

indicators.note: in places the bird inside the brotherhood, as a container

parts.note: an order is a fraternity or brotherhood, as of monks or knights
the swallow is a migrating bird

explanation.surface: A bird nesting among a Cornish brotherhood turns out to be a greedy eater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts SWALLOW inside ORDER, after SW for Cornwall's corner of England. The definition is witty: a performer who gulps down blades has, literally, a sharp appetite.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairground performer who gulps down blades could be said to relish keen-edged food.

clue.text: How treat a priest turbulent inmate

parts.note: Eli is the priest in the Book of Samuel, the crossword's stock priest

indicators.note: turbulent means disturbed and agitated, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A violent prisoner raises the old question of what to do with a meddlesome priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turbulent' rearranges INMATE into MINATE. The surface echoes Henry II's 'Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?', which led to Becket's murder.
explanation.definitionFit: To get rid of someone, as Henry II's knights did to Becket, is to kill or remove them.

clue.text: See 1 dn
A man, say, goes this way with his bride

definitions.text: goes this way with his bride

parts.note: the Isle of Man is an example of an island, an isle

explanation.surface: A bridegroom walks down the church with his new wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man' is printed lower case to hide the Isle of Man, an island in the Irish Sea; 'say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridegroom walks his new wife back down the central passage between the church pews.

clue.text: Mere turn by one of those magnificent men

definitions.text: by one of those magnificent men

indicators.note: turn tells us to turn the word round so it reads backwards

parts.note: a mere is a lake or pool

explanation.surface: An aviator from the old film does nothing more than a single turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mere' is a noun, a lake, not 'only'; POOL turned is the manoeuvre. 'Those Magnificent Men in their Flying Machines' is a 1965 film about early aviators, who would 'loop the loop'.
explanation.definitionFit: Early aviators were famous for flying a complete vertical circle, the stunt of 'looping the loop'.

clue.text: Beastly accommodation in the French manner

parts.note: L' is the French definite article cut short before a vowel
an air is a manner or bearing

explanation.surface: Rough lodgings described in a French style.
explanation.walkthrough: The elided French article L' (as in l'air) gives a single L.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild animal's den is where it lives, its home.

clue.text: One of Rovers' team transferred without fee ?

definitions.text: One of Rovers' team transferred without fee ?

parts.words: One of Rovers' team transferred without fee ?
parts.note: read as football, a player (a booter) moved on a free transfer; read another way, a member of a crew of rovers, that is pirates

explanation.walkthrough: Rovers is a common football club name, but a rover is also a pirate; split the answer as FREE BOOTER and it is a footballer signed for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirate or plundering adventurer is a rover; split, the word also suggests a kicker who cost nothing.

clue.text: Force in untried parts

indicators.note: parts suggests the word is broken up and its letters reassembled

explanation.surface: Troops are sent into areas nobody has yet tested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parts' rearranges UNTRIED; 'Force in' is a verb phrase, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To push oneself or something in where unwelcome is to barge in uninvited.

clue.text: Abode might be to let, dear

indicators.note: might be says the following letters could become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: A dear little house could well be up for rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abode' is not a house but the past tense of abide, to put up with; 'might be' rearranges TO LET DEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: To abide something is to bear or endure it, so its past form means endured.

clue.text: Music from Victoria ?

parts.note: Victoria is a London railway terminus, so what comes from it is locomotives and carriages; the word also means passages of melody

explanation.walkthrough: Victoria is a major London railway station. Its 'S plus what it sends out gives a word for musical passages.
explanation.definitionFit: Passages of a tune are melodies; split, the word gives the rail services leaving Victoria.

clue.text: Spanish ship detailed to carry one astronomer

indicators.note: to carry means the ship holds the next piece inside it
detailed means the word has its tail, its last letter, cut off

parts.note: a galleon is a Spanish sailing ship
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A Spanish vessel, shorn of its stern, takes on a stargazer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' cuts GALLEON to GALLEO, and 'to carry' puts I inside, after GAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian scientist who studied Jupiter's moons through his telescope was a famous stargazer.

clue.text: Leaderless, you two take fighting service to be obsolete

indicators.note: Leaderless means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: taken as written before losing its first letter
taken as written
RN is the Royal Navy, a fighting service

explanation.surface: Two people without a commander join the navy only to find it has had its day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaderless' takes the first letter off YOU, leaving OU.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worn out by long use is outdated and no longer of service.

clue.text: Yonder is a girl

parts.note: yonder means over there
's is a contraction of is

explanation.surface: Pointing, someone says: look over there, a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' shrinks to its contraction 's.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name stands for a girl.

clue.text: Engineer in well-equipped oriental galley

indicators.note: in puts the engineers inside the next word, as a container

parts.note: trim means in good order, well equipped
RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineers
E is the abbreviation for east, oriental

explanation.surface: A soldier-engineer is aboard a smart Eastern rowing ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts RE inside TRIM, after TRI.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient warship rowed by three banks of oarsmen is a kind of oared ship.

clue.text: Fashion class

definitions.meaning: to fashion is to shape or mould, a verb
a school class or year group, as in the sixth

explanation.definitionFit: One word covers both: to shape something, and a school year group in British schools.

clue.text: Case for reallocating duties in the Centre

indicators.note: reallocating means sharing out again, so the letters are rearranged
in the Centre takes only the inner letters of the word, dropping its first and last

explanation.surface: An argument for redistributing jobs at head office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the Centre' leaves UTIE from DUTIES, and 'reallocating' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: A small ornamental holder for needles and pins is a needlecase.

clue.text: Refuse a pound after start of horse race

indicators.note: after places the following pieces later in the answer than the start

parts.note: 'They're off!' marks the start of a horse race
L is the abbreviation for pound (libra)

explanation.surface: Someone turns down a pound bet as the race gets under way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start of horse race' looks like it picks the letter H; it is the whole word OFF, the call when racers break.
explanation.definitionFit: Refuse as a noun is waste; offal is entrails and discarded parts of a carcass.

clue.text: Person of high degree

parts.note: high degree reads as social rank but means the top class of university degree

explanation.walkthrough: A first-class degree is the highest British undergraduate classification; someone who holds one is called by its short name.
explanation.definitionFit: A graduate with top honours is said to have, or be, a top-class degree holder.

clue.text: They came but went not for Caesar

definitions.text: They came but went not for Caesar

parts.words: They came but went not for Caesar
parts.note: Caesar says to the soothsayer that a fateful day of March has come, and is told 'Ay, Caesar, but not gone'

explanation.walkthrough: From Julius Caesar: 'The ides of March are come.' 'Ay, Caesar; but not gone.' He was killed that day.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman calendar's mid-month day in March was the date of Caesar's assassination.

clue.text: Greatly disliked one's cover notes

parts.note: a hat covers one's head
E and D are musical notes

explanation.surface: Someone hated the notes on the cover of a record.
explanation.walkthrough: E and D are two of the musical notes A to G.
explanation.definitionFit: Something strongly disliked is loathed or detested.

clue.text: Run finished with cast upset

parts.note: something that has run its course is over, finished
to throw is to cast

explanation.surface: The run of a play ended and the cast were unhappy.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an overthrow is also a run conceded by a wild return, hinted at by 'Run'.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset a government is to bring it down or topple it.

clue.text: Setting right radio smashed by this ?

definitions.text: Setting right radio smashed by this ?

indicators.note: smashed means broken up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something that would wreck a radio is being set up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smashed' rearranges SETTING, R and RADIO. The whole clue also defines: a destructive device would smash the radio.
explanation.definitionFit: A device that breaks things into fragments would smash a radio.
